narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the model predicts a 96% chance you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. In practical terms, this means that out of 100 students with a similar profile, only about 4 would be expected to pass, which the admissions committee considered too high a risk to accept.

Three factors, in order of importance, drove this decision. The most influential was your class standing in the third year of undergraduate study. You ranked in the lowest decile (1 out of 10), while accepted students typically sat around the 6th decile. This pattern is strongly associated with bar exam failure because third-year performance reflects your mastery of advanced legal material. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 24, far below the average of 37 among accepted applicants. The LSAT is designed to predict first-year law school success and, by extension, bar passage, so a score this low points to significant difficulty with the analytical and reading skills the exam requires. The third factor, though smaller in influence, was your first-year class rank. Like your third-year rank, you were in the bottom decile, compared with an average of around 6th decile for accepted students. Early struggles in your academic record compound the concern.

All three of these signals point in the same direction: toward bar exam failure. Your middle-class family income and full-time enrollment status were not decisive factors in this prediction.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic standing, particularly in your final undergraduate years, and consider dedicated LSAT preparation or a prep course to substantially increase your score before reapplying.
